analysis.one_liner: Taxes high earners' investment and business income at 3.8% to shore up Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 57 cosponsors alongside its sponsor, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 22, 2025 and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill keeps a 3.8% tax on investment income but changes who pays it: the tax would start at incomes above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples) instead of today's $200,000, and it would also apply to profits that high earners take out of their own businesses — S corporations and partnerships — which currently escape it. All the money raised would go into the trust fund that pays Medicare's hospital bills (Part A). It was sent to the tax-writing committee and has sat there since.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Medicare beneficiaries, whose hospital coverage (Part A) is funded by the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund. The bill pours all revenue from this tax into that fund, which helps keep hospital benefits solvent as more of the population retires. Working people who earn wages benefit indirectly: the bill closes a gap that lets high earners reclassify their pay as business profits and avoid the Medicare tax that wage earners cannot avoid.

how_it_helps.text: All revenue from the 3.8% net investment tax would be deposited into the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, the fund that pays Medicare Part A hospital bills, starting with tax years after 2025.

The tax would begin at modified adjusted gross income above $400,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers, roughly double the current thresholds of $200,000 and $250,000 — meaning the tax is aimed squarely at the top of the income scale.

For people above those thresholds, the tax would apply to the greater of investment income or 'specified net income,' which sweeps in business profits from S corporations and partnerships, income from investing working capital, gains from selling business property, and certain foreign income — closing the main path by which high earners' business income currently escapes the 3.8% tax.

The bill disallows net operating losses from being used to reduce the investment tax base, and directs the IRS to issue guidance on corporate distributions and previously taxed income so the expanded tax can be administered.
Wages already subject to Medicare payroll tax, and income already covered by self-employment tax, are excluded, so the tax targets income streams that currently pay neither.

analysis.who_pays: Households with incomes over $400,000 ($500,000 for joint filers), plus estates and trusts — especially owners of S corporations and partnerships whose business profits currently avoid the 3.8% investment tax. A phase-in limits the added tax on the first $100,000 of income above the threshold, softening the initial hit. No one below those income levels pays anything under the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and business owners over $400k

drawbacks.text: The tax would reach the active business income of professionals and owners of S corporations and partnerships earning over $400,000 — doctors, lawyers, and family business owners organized as pass-throughs — who argue that income is compensation for work, not passive investment. The bill's phase-in limits the increase on the first $100,000 of income above the threshold, but larger earners above that would face the full tax.

Dedicating the revenue only to the Part A hospital trust fund does nothing about Medicare's overall costs — prescription drug prices, insurer payments, or physician fees — so the bill addresses one solvency problem while leaving the rest of the program untouched.

The expanded tax adds real complexity: disallowing net operating losses against investment income, pulling in foreign-sourced income, and requiring new IRS guidance on corporate distributions and previously taxed income all create compliance work for filers and administrative work for the IRS.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a steady new stream of dedicated funding for Medicare's hospital insurance fund, paid entirely by households above $400,000/$500,000 and by closing the pass-through loophole that lets high earners dodge the Medicare tax wage earners pay. The costs are real but narrow: a higher tax bill for affluent business owners and professionals, and a more complicated tax code for high-income filers and the IRS. There is no cost to people below the income thresholds. The main weakness is design scope — it shores up one trust fund rather than Medicare's cost problem overall — but as a solvency measure its burden falls where the money is.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and has not moved since — no hearing, no vote, nothing — while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on January 22, 2025, joined by 57 original cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — has been taken, and there is no Senate companion bill in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and owners of S corporations and partnerships are better off so far, because the tax that would apply to their business profits has gone nowhere. The Part A trust fund is also no closer to new dedicated revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners whose business income stays untaxed

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 57 Democratic cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 57 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Members of the House Progressive Caucus and allied Democrats, including Ms. Jayapal, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, Mr. Khanna, and Ms. Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, all 57 as Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its referral on January 22, 2025.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agenda
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor process have not advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 House sponsors — the sponsor plus 57 cosponsors — are Democrats; not a single Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling Ways and Means, the bill has stayed in committee.

industries.industry: Owners of S corporations and partnerships (law, medicine, finance, and other professional practices)
industries.note: The bill's core change taxes the business profits of owners earning over $400,000, which today escape the 3.8% investment tax because they are treated as active business income rather than investment income. That is precisely the income the bill targets to fund Medicare, so the industry's interest runs directly against the bill's public purpose.

Estates, trusts, and individuals above the new $400,000/$500,000 thresholds would owe the 3.8% tax on a broader income base, including foreign-sourced income and gains on business property, and could no longer offset it with net operating losses.

Dedicating the tax revenue to the Part A trust fund stabilizes the payer that covers a large share of hospital revenue, which matters for hospitals' finances and for patients' continued access to covered care.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support, no Senate companion in the record, and the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee having taken no action in the year since referral, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress. Its most plausible route forward is as a provision inside a larger tax or reconciliation package if Democrats regain control of an agenda-setting body, which is not the current situation.
